newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh's Khaleda says won't harm development.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh's Khaleda says won't harm development.

text.p: Bangladesh's main opposition leader, Begum Khaleda Zia, said on Saturday that her Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) would not stand in the way of development.

"We intend to ensure political stability for the sake of the well-being of our people. We are not ones who would create any obstacle in the way of development for the sake of party politics," Khaleda told a luncheon meeting of American businesses in Bangladesh.
"I take great pride of reassuring that our politics is not of vengeance but of extending hands of cooperation to anyone who believes in the basic concept of democratic governnance ...," she said.

Khaleda's statement on Saturday could provide some reassurance for the government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, which is trying to retain an investment-friendly atmosphere in the impoverished country.
Awami League chief Hasina, who defeated Khaleda's BNP in parliamentary elections last June, recently blamed her principal rival for sabotaging development efforts.
Khaleda also stated publicly that she would soon launch a vigorous campaign to topple what she called was Hasina's "corrupt, inefficient and repressive government".
The BNP chief said on Saturday that foreign investors were rather alarmed by economic management of the government and its "politicisation of business, trade and commerce".

"We had not done anything to destabilise the political and social environement, but the government has so messed up the economy, including the money market, that no genuine foreign investor has really started up any investment yet," Khaleda said.
"BNP extends its hands of cooperation to all investors who are helping our nation-building efforts," she told the luncheon meeting of the American Chamber of Commerce in Bangladesh.

The 10-month-old government of Sheikh Hasina has been criticised by the opposition over recent crash in the stock market and lately by the central bank governor's alarming disclosure about the limping banking sector.
While pledging her cooperation, the former prime minister, however, asked the ruling Awami League to shun "persecution and harassment" of her followers.
"Let us hope that the present government would get above the politics of rhetorics, politics of persecution and harassment and the politics of money and violence," she said.
Khaleda alleged that more than 150 BNP leaders and workers had been killed in last 10 months and thousands others arrested or harassed.

"There are instances of clear violation of basic human rights. We want an immediate end to this situation, so that we can rightfully, and without fear, discharge our duties as a responsible and the biggest ever opposition in thh Parliament."
Khaleda on Saturday, however, made no mention of her demand for removal of the Chief Election Commissioner Abu Hena, whom she termed as partisan towards the Awami League.
"He has not only failed to hold free and fair polls but he is also partisan," the Independent quoted former prime minister Khaleda as telling her supporters on Friday.
She said Hena, a retired bureaucrat, should be replaced by a Supreme Court judge to ensure fairness in future polls.
Khaleda alleged Hena had "helped the Awami League to win the (June 1996) elections" and vowed not to participate in future polls unless he is dismissed.
Hena has rejected the BNP's charge as baseless.
